title: Arizona Special District Websites: ADA Title II PDF Accessibility | SignalFeed.dev
description: How Arizona special-district websites stand on PDF accessibility before the April 26, 2028 ADA Title II date: 58% of 549 sampled PDFs untagged, 38% scanned. Aggregate, automated signals.
h1: Arizona: Title II PDF backlog on special district websites
body:
We found 14 working special-district websites (transit, water, fire, park, library and similar districts) on .gov domains registered in Arizona in CISA's public .gov registry. Special districts are Title II public entities; under the ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H) special district governments have until April 26, 2028 to make web content, PDFs included, conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, subject to the rule's exceptions.

Does ADA Title II apply to Arizona?

Yes. Title II is federal law and covers Arizona's state agencies and public universities, counties, cities, towns, school districts and special districts; the PDF guide covers the rule's exceptions. This is general information, not legal advice.

We measured the PDFs these sites link from their pages. This page summarizes Arizona's special-district sites as a whole. It does not name or rank individual districts. Districts without a registered .gov domain are not included. For cities and counties, see the city and county editions.

Arizona at a glance

  • 10 of 14 special-district sites measured with a usable sample (20 or more PDFs). Of the rest, 0 blocked our crawler and 4 could not be sampled: too few PDFs on the main site (some host documents on other systems) or a crawl that only partly finished. That is not a clean result.
  • 549 PDFs analyzed. 58.3% had no accessibility tags, higher than the national figure of 40.0%. 37.5% were scanned images with no usable text, 59.9% did not declare a document language, and 68% had no document title.
  • Spread: in 5 of the 10 measured districts more than half the sampled PDFs were untagged; in none, fewer than 1 in 10 were. The most common main issue was missing accessibility tags (7 of 10 districts).
  • 0 of 30 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • The median measured site has roughly 855 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check; across the measured sites that is on the order of 18,000 pages.
  • 45% of the sampled PDFs were modified in 2024 or later. Recent documents are more likely to still be in active use, and documents used to apply for, access or participate in a service are not covered by the rule's exception for preexisting documents.

What this means for Arizona special districts

An untagged PDF gives a screen reader no headings, reading order or table structure, and a scanned one gives it nothing; both typically fail WCAG 2.1 AA and are common in board agendas, budgets, rate notices and forms. Archived content and preexisting documents are exempt unless people use them to get a service, so the usual order is: fix export settings, remediate forms and service documents, then move true archives to a marked archive section.

For agendas, minutes and notices, our accessible meeting templates for small public bodies ($24, Word + PDF/UA) export tagged PDFs from Word, so new documents start out accessible.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals scaled from samples, not a conformance evaluation: a check can show a PDF fails, not that it conforms. Method: national Backlog Index page.

Per-site data

The Arizona workbook lists every special-district site we targeted in the state, with the registering organization, with PDFs found and estimated, untagged and scanned shares, recent-document share, estimated pages failing basic checks and days to the compliance date.
